questions.question: In a three-tier campus design, which tier connects end-user devices?
questions.explanation: Access switches connect PCs, phones, and APs.

correct.explanation: The access tier connects end-user devices — PCs, phones, and access ports on switches/APs.

incorrect.explanation: Core provides high-speed backbone between distribution blocks — not direct end-user attachment.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Connecting users at the core tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Core points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "access tier", Access satisfies what this question tests — Core does not.

incorrect.explanation: Distribution aggregates access switches and applies policy — users connect at access, not distribution.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Placing user ports in distribution tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Distribution points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "access tier", Access satisfies what this question tests — Distribution does not.

incorrect.explanation: Spine is a data-center fabric term — campus three-tier uses access/distribution/core.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Mixing DC spine-leaf with campus access tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spine points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "access tier", Access satisfies what this question tests — Spine does not.

answerReview.examTip: Campus three-tier: Access = users. Distribution = policy/aggregation. Core = backbone.

questions.question: Spine-leaf architecture is primarily used for…
questions.explanation: Spine-leaf fabrics optimize predictable, scalable traffic between servers in data centers.

correct.explanation: Spine-leaf provides full bisection bandwidth for east-west (server-to-server) traffic in data centers.

incorrect.explanation: SOHO Wi-Fi uses a single AP/router — not a multi-spine fabric design.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying DC fabric to home Wi-Fi
incorrect.whatItDoes: SOHO Wi‑Fi points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "spine-leaf", Data center east-west traffic satisfies what this question tests — SOHO Wi‑Fi does not.

incorrect.explanation: Dial-up WAN is legacy remote access — unrelated to spine-leaf DC switching.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing WAN dial-up with DC architecture
incorrect.whatItDoes: Dial-up WAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "spine-leaf", Data center east-west traffic satisfies what this question tests — Dial-up WAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: Home gaming does not require spine-leaf — that architecture targets scalable DC east-west traffic.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using DC design for consumer gaming
incorrect.whatItDoes: Home gaming points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "spine-leaf", Data center east-west traffic satisfies what this question tests — Home gaming does not.

answerReview.examTip: Spine-leaf = data center east-west scalability. Campus = access/distribution/core.

questions.question: Ten branch offices send all WAN traffic through headquarters. Which topology is this?
questions.explanation: All spokes via one hub = hub-and-spoke.

correct.explanation: All branches home through headquarters — classic hub-and-spoke WAN topology.

incorrect.explanation: Full mesh connects every site to every other site — not all traffic through one HQ hub.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing hub-spoke with full mesh
incorrect.whatItDoes: Full mesh points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hub-spoke", Hub-and-spoke satisfies what this question tests — Full mesh does not.

incorrect.explanation: Spine-leaf is a data-center L2/L3 fabric — not the branch WAN pattern described.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying DC fabric to branch WAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spine-leaf points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hub-spoke", Hub-and-spoke satisfies what this question tests — Spine-leaf does not.

incorrect.explanation: Point-to-point is one link between two sites — ten branches via HQ is hub-and-spoke.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Calling multi-branch HQ model point-to-point only
incorrect.whatItDoes: Point-to-point only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hub-spoke", Hub-and-spoke satisfies what this question tests — Point-to-point only does not.

answerReview.examTip: All branches → HQ = hub-and-spoke. Every site ↔ every site = full mesh.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of a full-mesh WAN?
questions.explanation: Full mesh connects every site to every other — resilient but expensive.

correct.explanation: Full mesh needs n(n−1)/2 links — cost and complexity explode as sites grow.

incorrect.explanation: Full mesh maximizes redundancy — the trade-off is cost/complexity, not lack of redundancy.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing mesh removes redundancy
incorrect.whatItDoes: No redundancy points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "full mesh", High cost/complexity for many links satisfies what this question tests — No redundancy does not.

incorrect.explanation: Mesh works over various transports — it is not limited to fiber only.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Restricting mesh to one media type
incorrect.whatItDoes: Only works with fiber points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "full mesh", High cost/complexity for many links satisfies what this question tests — Only works with fiber does not.

incorrect.explanation: Routing still runs over mesh links — mesh describes topology, not elimination of routing.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Thinking mesh removes routing protocols
incorrect.whatItDoes: Eliminates routing points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "full mesh", High cost/complexity for many links satisfies what this question tests — Eliminates routing does not.

answerReview.examTip: Full mesh = max redundancy, max cost. Hub-spoke = cheaper, single point at hub.

questions.question: A collapsed core campus design has how many tiers?
questions.explanation: Two-tier merges distribution and core — access + collapsed distribution/core.

correct.explanation: Collapsed core merges distribution and core into two tiers: collapsed core + access.

incorrect.explanation: One tier would be a flat network — collapsed core still has access and a combined core/distribution layer.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Calling collapsed core a single-tier design
incorrect.whatItDoes: One points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "two-tier", Two satisfies what this question tests — One does not.

incorrect.explanation: Four tiers exceed standard collapsed-core models — collapsed means fewer tiers than classic three-tier.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Adding extra tiers to collapsed design
incorrect.whatItDoes: Four points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "two-tier", Two satisfies what this question tests — Four does not.

incorrect.explanation: Five tiers is not a standard campus model — collapsed core reduces to two functional tiers.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Inventing non-standard tier count
incorrect.whatItDoes: Five points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "two-tier", Two satisfies what this question tests — Five does not.

answerReview.examTip: Collapsed core = 2 tiers (access + collapsed core/distribution). Classic = 3 tiers.

questions.question: A home user has one wireless router providing NAT, DHCP, and Wi‑Fi. This is typical of…
questions.explanation: Small office/home office networks are simple, often one integrated gateway.

correct.explanation: A single wireless router providing NAT, DHCP, and Wi‑Fi is classic SOHO (small office/home office).

incorrect.explanation: Core datacenter uses redundant spine-leaf, not a single consumer router.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: SOHO as core datacenter
incorrect.whatItDoes: Core datacenter points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wireless.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wireless", SOHO satisfies what this question tests — Core datacenter does not.

incorrect.explanation: Full mesh WAN connects every site to every other site — not a home router.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: SOHO as full mesh WAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: Full mesh WAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wireless.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wireless", SOHO satisfies what this question tests — Full mesh WAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: Spine-leaf fabric is datacenter switching — SOHO is one integrated gateway.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: SOHO as spine fabric
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spine fabric points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wireless.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wireless", SOHO satisfies what this question tests — Spine fabric does not.

answerReview.examTip: SOHO = all-in-one gateway (NAT + DHCP + Wi‑Fi) | Enterprise = layered, redundant design.

questions.question: In which cloud model does the customer manage the operating system but not the physical hardware?
questions.explanation: IaaS provides VMs/infrastructure; the customer manages OS and above.

correct.explanation: IaaS — customer manages the OS and apps; provider supplies compute, storage, and network hardware.

incorrect.explanation: SaaS — provider manages everything including the application (e.g., Office 365).
incorrect.misconceptionTested: SaaS customer manages OS
incorrect.whatItDoes: SaaS points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud model.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud model", IaaS satisfies what this question tests — SaaS does not.

incorrect.explanation: PaaS — provider manages OS/runtime; customer deploys code only.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: PaaS customer manages OS
incorrect.whatItDoes: PaaS points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud model.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud model", IaaS satisfies what this question tests — PaaS does not.

incorrect.explanation: On-prem means customer owns all hardware — not a cloud model.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: On-prem as cloud model
incorrect.whatItDoes: On-prem only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud model.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud model", IaaS satisfies what this question tests — On-prem only does not.

answerReview.examTip: Cloud stack: IaaS (you manage OS) → PaaS (you manage code) → SaaS (you use app).

questions.question: True or False: In spine-leaf, each leaf switch connects to every spine switch.
questions.explanation: True — full mesh between leaves and spines is the defining property.

correct.explanation: True — in spine-leaf, every leaf connects to every spine for equal-cost paths.

incorrect.explanation: False is wrong — full mesh between leaf and spine is the defining spine-leaf trait.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Spine-leaf partial connectivity
incorrect.whatItDoes: False states the opposite of the tested fact about spine connectivity.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "spine connectivity", True satisfies what this question tests — False does not.

answerReview.examTip: Spine-leaf: leaves = access/aggregation | spines = core — every leaf ↔ every spine.
